opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the two are actually pretty closely connected. The way we originally framed multi-agent debate was really as an inference-time procedure. You take a model that's already trained, you instantiate several copies of it, or even different models, and you have each one propose an answer. Then they read each other's responses, critique them, and update their own reasoning over a few rounds. What we found is that even without changing any weights, this process tends to converge on answers that are more factually accurate and have better reasoning. Hallucinations tend to get filtered out, because if one agent makes something up, the others often don't agree with it, and it gets challenged.

But once you have a procedure that reliably produces better answers than the base model would produce on its own, the natural next question is: why not use that as a training signal? The debate process essentially gives you an improved distribution of outputs. You can then distill that back into the model, fine-tuning it on the answers and reasoning traces that emerged from the debate. So the model internalizes some of what it would have gotten from talking with other agents, and you don't have to pay the inference cost of running multiple agents every time.

And I think what's exciting is that this can become iterative. You train the model on debate outputs, now it's a stronger model, you run debate again with the improved models, you get even better outputs, and you distill again. It's a kind of self-improvement loop. One thing we've found important there is maintaining diversity among the agents. If you just fine-tune everything on the same consensus answers, the models collapse toward each other, and then debate stops being useful because everyone agrees from the start. So you want to specialize the agents a bit, some generating answers, some acting as critics, trained on different slices of data, so that the debate stays informative.

So I see it as a spectrum. At inference time, debate is a way to spend more compute to get a better answer right now. During training, it's a way to turn that extra compute into a permanently better model. And they reinforce each other: better models make for better debates, and better debates make for better training data.

r001.rationale: The response describes agents critiquing and challenging one another’s answers to improve answer quality, then using the resulting debate outputs as a training signal through distillation. It presents debate as improving answers both at inference and during training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of them as two sides of the same coin, and the interesting thing is that they actually feed into each other.

So when we first did the multi-agent debate work, the framing was really the inference-time side. You have a frozen language model, you spin up several copies of it, each gives an answer, and then they read each other's answers and revise. And what you find is that the final answer after a few rounds is more accurate and more factual than any single sample, and often more accurate than just doing majority voting over the same number of samples. The intuition is that models are much better at verifying or critiquing an answer than they are at generating a correct one from scratch, so debate lets you convert that verification ability into better generation. It's basically a way of spending more compute at test time to get a better answer out of the model you already have.

The training-time view is: well, if the debate output is systematically better than what a single model produces, that's a supervision signal. You've essentially bootstrapped a slightly stronger model out of a weaker one, and you can distill that back in. So you run debates, take the consensus or the final revised answers, and fine-tune the base model on them. The hope is that the single model now produces in one shot what previously took several agents and several rounds. And then you can iterate, debate again with the improved model, distill again, and so on.

What I find appealing about this is that it's a route to self-improvement that doesn't require a human to label anything. The signal comes from the structure of the interaction, from the fact that disagreement between agents exposes errors that no single agent would catch on its own.

There are some subtleties, though. One is diversity. Debate works because the agents make different mistakes. If you distill too aggressively, you can collapse that diversity, and then debate at inference time gives you less and less, because the agents just agree with each other immediately, even when they're wrong. So in some of the follow-up work we looked at keeping a population of models with different roles or different training histories rather than one homogeneous set, precisely to preserve that.

The other thing is that I don't think training ever fully replaces inference-time debate. There's always going to be a frontier of problems that the single model can't solve in one pass, and for those you want the ability to deliberate, to have multiple perspectives interact and check each other. So the way I'd put it is: training on debate pushes up the baseline of what the model gets right instantly, and inference-time debate is what you reach for at the edge of that baseline. The two together give you a kind of ratchet, where each round of training raises the floor and each round of debate lets you reach a bit higher than the floor.

r001.rationale: The response explains that agents critique and verify answers to improve them during inference, then uses the resulting stronger debate answers as supervision for training. This conveys answer-quality feedback as the mechanism shared by both approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re complementary. After training, you can have multiple models propose answers, critique one another, and revise their responses. That gives you a way to improve an answer by spending more computation at inference time, without changing the models’ weights.

But you can also use that process to generate training data. If the discussion produces a better answer, you can train a model on that answer so that, ideally, it learns to produce it directly, without needing the whole debate every time. So one way to think about it is that debate lets you explore better answers, and training lets you absorb some of those improvements into the model.

The challenge in both cases is deciding whether the answer actually got better. Agreement isn’t necessarily correctness—models can reinforce a shared mistake. So having some way to verify the outcome is really valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says debate can produce answers for inference-time revision or training, and that verifying whether an answer improved is valuable. It does not identify feedback about answer quality as the shared mechanism that enables improvement in both settings.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re very complementary. You can use debate after training by having several models propose answers, critique one another, and revise their responses. That lets you spend more computation on a question without changing the models themselves.

But you can also use that process to generate training data. If the discussion produces a better answer, you can train a model on that answer, essentially trying to internalize some of the benefit of debate. Then, at inference time, you might get a stronger initial response without needing the whole discussion every time.

The important caveat is that agreement doesn’t necessarily mean correctness. Models can share the same misconception or persuade one another of something wrong. So, in both settings, you want ways to check whether the debate actually improves the answer, rather than just making the models converge.

r001.rationale: The response describes debate, critique, revision, and using better debate answers as training data, but it does not clearly identify feedback about answer quality as the shared mechanism enabling improvement in both settings.
